The Shimofuri goby, Tridentiger bifasciatus, is a brackish-water species with a compressed life history typical of small-bodied gobiids. Field surveys indicate that sexual maturation occurs when individuals reach a standard length of 3.7 cm [Lp = 3.7 cm], a point at which gonadal recrudescence is first observed and individuals transition from the juvenile phase to reproductive viability. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs that measure approximately 0.79 mm in diameter, yielding an extremely modest wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00026 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00026 grams] upon eclosion from the chorion. This scant initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic prolarva, which must rapidly develop mouth gape and retinal differentiation to commence first exogenous feeding within a few days post-hatch. The species' small body size at maturity, paired with the minimal investment per offspring, aligns with a ruderal life-history strategy common among gobies that colonise ephemeral estuarine habitats and face substantial early-life mortality.

Comparative growth data derived from field-collected specimens suggest that maximum recorded body size in adults reaches approximately 9.96 cm [Li = approximately 9.96 cm] in ultimate standard length, a value estimated from individuals whose total length measured around 12 cm. This asymptotic length is consistent with values reported for other congeners within the genus Tridentiger, although it falls at the smaller end of the range for gobiids occupying similar ecological niches in East Asian estuaries. By late summer, the largest reproductively active adults captured in seine nets and visual surveys approached this upper limit, with females typically attaining slightly greater lengths than males. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an adult of this size is calculated at approximately 30.14 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.14 grams], reflecting a thickset body morphology with firm musculature adapted for benthic foraging among cobble and shell substrates. This body mass is achieved through a period of sustained feeding on polychaetes, amphipods, and small crustaceans throughout the warmer months, with growth decelerating markedly as the fish approach their maximum size.

The documented lifespan of the Shimofuri goby is notably brief, with available data indicating that individuals typically survive for approximately 547 days [am = approximately 547 days] under natural conditions when maintained at water temperatures averaging 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively short longevity is characteristic of small-bodied gobiids that experience intense predation pressure from larger piscivores such as juvenile Lateolabrax japonicus and estuarine birds. Mark-recapture studies conducted over consecutive spawning seasons in the tidal creeks of Tokyo Bay confirmed that very few tagged fish were recovered beyond a second winter, with the majority of the population turning over on an annual cycle. The compressed lifespan places strong selective pressure on early maturation and high reproductive output within the first breeding season, as many individuals will not survive to spawn in a subsequent year. Senescent adult death typically follows the post-spawning period, with physiological deterioration accelerating as water temperatures decline in late autumn.

Laboratory rearing experiments provide additional context for the species' early ontogeny and size at maturation. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva weighs 0.00026 grams [Wwb = 0.00026 grams] at a standard water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a value derived from volumetric approximations based on the measured egg diameter of 0.79 mm. This initial wet weight is among the lowest recorded for gobiids in temperate Asian waters, comparable only to those of Gymnogobius species that produce similarly diminutive adhesive eggs. Following the transition to exogenous feeding and the completion of the exotrophic larval phase, individuals undergo a pelagic-benthic transition and begin the juvenile growth trajectory. The small size at birth imposes a steep growth trajectory if the fish are to reach the 3.7 cm [Lp = 3.7 cm] standard length at puberty within the first summer, a challenge that is met through high ingestion rates during the warmwater months when prey densities peak in the shallow littoral zone.

Adult body mass also offers insight into the species' reproductive energetics. The calculated asymptotic wet weight of approximately 30.14 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.14 grams] for the largest individuals represents a substantial multiplier over the 0.00026 gram [Wwb = 0.00026 gram] hatchling wet weight, reflecting a more than 115,000-fold increase in somatic mass over the course of development. Most of this mass gain occurs during the juvenile and young adult stages, with growth rates declining sharply after the attainment of the ultimate standard length of 9.96 cm [Li = 9.96 cm]. Field collections of gravid females from rocky shorelines in the Yangtze River estuary confirmed that individuals nearing this maximum size carried the largest ovarian masses, suggesting that the energetic surplus available after somatic growth plateaus is redirected toward vitellogenesis and egg production. This pattern is consistent with an income-breeding strategy in which food intake during the spawning season directly fuels gamete development, rather than drawing on stored lipid reserves, a strategy well-suited to the productive but seasonally pulsed food supply of estuarine environments.
